difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — a single deduction from the shape of an increase-then-decrease function (equal values only on opposite sides of the peak); about a minute.
stem:
Weight of a person can be expressed as a function of their age. The function usually varies from person to person. Suppose this function is identical for two brothers, and it monotonically increases till the age of 50 years and then it monotonically decreases. Let $a_1$ and $a_2$ (in years) denote the ages of the brothers and $a_1 < a_2$.

Which one of the following statements is correct about their age on the day when they attain the same weight?

solution.quick: Let $w(a)$ be the common weight function: increasing up to age 50 and decreasing after it. On the same side of 50, two different ages always give different weights, and age 50 gives the unique maximum weight. So equal weights force the ages to lie on opposite sides of the peak: $a_1 < 50 < a_2$, option **(B)**.

steps.title: Set up the condition
steps.body:
Let $w(a)$ be the weight at age $a$, the same function for both brothers. It increases on ages up to 50 and decreases after 50, so $w(50)$ is the largest weight either brother ever has. On the day in question the brothers have different ages $a_1 < a_2$ and

$$w(a_1) = w(a_2).$$

We test where $a_1$ and $a_2$ can lie relative to 50 (the monotonicity is taken as strict: weight keeps changing with age, as the question intends).

steps.title: Both ages at most 50 — rules out (A)
steps.body: If $a_1 < a_2 \le 50$, both ages are on the increasing part, so $w(a_1) < w(a_2)$: the elder brother is strictly heavier. The weights cannot be equal, so $a_1 < a_2 < 50$ is impossible.

steps.title: Both ages at least 50 — rules out (C)
steps.body: If $50 \le a_1 < a_2$, both ages are on the decreasing part, so $w(a_1) > w(a_2)$: the younger brother is strictly heavier. Again the weights cannot be equal, so $50 < a_1 < a_2$ is impossible.

steps.title: One brother exactly 50 — rules out (D)
steps.body: $w(50)$ is the peak. If $a_1 = 50$, then $a_2 > 50$ gives $w(a_2) < w(50)$; if $a_2 = 50$, then $a_1 < 50$ gives $w(a_1) < w(50)$. Either way the weights differ, so (D) is impossible.

steps.title: Only one case remains — (B)
steps.body:
The only possibility left is $a_1 < 50 < a_2$: the younger brother is still on the rising part of the curve and the elder is already on the falling part. This case really can occur — for example, if weight rose and fell at the same rate, ages 40 and 60 would give equal weights. Any horizontal line below the peak cuts the curve once on each side of 50.

Answer: **(B)**.

solution.teaching:
A function is **strictly increasing** on an interval if a larger input always gives a larger output, and **strictly decreasing** if a larger input always gives a smaller output. Either way, the function is **one-to-one** on that interval: two *different* inputs can never produce the *same* output there.

The weight function in this question is **unimodal**: it climbs up to a single peak (age 50) and then falls. Such a function is not one-to-one overall, but it is one-to-one on each side of the peak separately. Picture the graph as a hill and draw a horizontal line at some weight below the summit: it meets the hill exactly twice, once on the way up and once on the way down. At the summit itself the line touches only once, because the peak value is attained only at age 50.

Now apply this to two people who share the same weight curve but have different ages. Equal weight means the same height on the hill at two different points. Two points on the same slope are at different heights, and the summit is higher than every other point, so the only way to be at the same height is to be on **opposite slopes**. Hence the peak age lies strictly between the two ages: $a_1 < 50 < a_2$.

The same reasoning appears in data science whenever a quantity rises and then falls (for example, validation accuracy as model complexity grows): two different settings with the same value must lie on opposite sides of the optimum.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Both ages are on the increasing part of the curve, so the elder brother (age $a_2$) is strictly heavier; equal weight is impossible.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The younger brother is on the rising part and the elder on the falling part of the same curve; only in this configuration can two different ages give the same weight.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Both ages are on the decreasing part, so the younger brother (age $a_1$) is strictly heavier; equal weight is impossible.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: At age 50 the weight is the unique maximum, so the brother who is 50 would be strictly heavier than his brother of a different age; the weights cannot be equal.

solution.shortcut: For an up-then-down function, equal values at two different points can occur only on opposite sides of the peak, so the peak age 50 lies strictly between $a_1$ and $a_2$.
solution.commonTrap: Picking (D) because 50 is the ‘special’ age in the question. Age 50 is where weight is highest, so a brother aged exactly 50 is strictly heavier than his brother; the special age must lie *between* the two ages, not equal one of them.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); gap={'A':np.inf,'C':np.inf,'D':np.inf}; B_equal=0
for _ in range(20):  # random weight curves: strictly up till 50, strictly down after
    up,dn=rng.uniform(0.1,2,2); w=lambda a:np.where(a<=50,up*a,up*50-dn*(a-50))
    ages=np.arange(1,100,0.5)
    for a1 in ages:
        for a2 in ages[ages>a1]:
            c='A' if a2<50 else 'C' if a1>50 else 'D' if 50 in (a1,a2) else 'B'
            if c!='B': gap[c]=min(gap[c],abs(w(a1)-w(a2)))
        if a1<50: a2=50+up*(50-a1)/dn; B_equal+= abs(w(a1)-w(a2))<1e-9 and a2>50  # partner with same weight
print('min |w(a1)-w(a2)| in cases A,C,D (never 0):',gap); print('equal-weight pairs found with a1<50<a2:',B_equal)
answerVerification.notes: Independent deduction ((A), (C), (D) contradict strict monotonicity on each side of the peak; only $a_1 < 50 < a_2$ allows equal weights) gives (B), agreeing with the official key B. The Python check samples random strictly increasing-then-decreasing weight curves with peak at 50: the weight gap never reaches 0 in the cases of options (A), (C) and (D), while equal-weight pairs with $a_1 < 50 < a_2$ exist.
